title: Severe Weather and Extreme Temperatures Procedure
summary: How we prepare for and respond to hot weather, cold weather, snow and ice, flooding, storms and weather-related loss of power or water: receiving and cascading UKHSA weather-health alerts and weather warnings, identifying people at higher weather risk, the checks care workers make in people's homes, keeping staff safe on the road and at work, and protecting essential visits when weather disrupts the service. For all staff.

keyPoints.intro: Heat, cold, snow, ice and flooding put the people we support and you at risk. These are the checks you make on visits and the rules that keep you safe when the weather turns.
points: Never make a journey you judge unsafe in snow, ice, flooding or high wind, and never walk or drive through floodwater. Phone the office or On-call Manager as soon as you know which visits you cannot reach. Nobody will pressure or penalise you.

During any heat-health or cold-health alert, read the room thermometer at every visit to a person shown at higher weather risk in My care at a glance, and record the reading and what you did in the daily visit notes.

In heat-health alerts, offer extra drinks and, unless fluids are restricted, leave at least two within reach. Above 26°C, close sunny curtains, open windows only when cooler outside and the care plan allows, and use a fan only below 35°C, never aimed at the person.

Below 18°C in the living room or bedroom: with the person's agreement, switch the heating on with its normal controls and help with layers, blankets and a hot drink. Never repair, reset or relight a boiler, fire or heater.

Phone the office before you leave if the room is still above 26°C or below 18°C for someone at higher weather risk, is 35°C or above for anyone, or the heating is not working, has no credit or fuel, or is declined.

Call 999 for heatstroke (still unwell after 30 minutes of cooling, hot dry skin, confusion, a fit or collapse) or possible hypothermia (pale cold skin with slurred speech, slow breathing, drowsiness or confusion). Keep them cool or gently warm, then phone the office.

Keep medicines below 25°C and out of the sun. Tell the office before you leave if the person is running short of medicines, food or drinks, or a power cut affects their powered equipment. Never change equipment settings.
In hot weather, drink water between every visit and take your breaks somewhere cool. Change gloves, aprons and masks when they become damp, but never go without the protection the care plan requires.

During a severe weather response, phone or text the office or On-call Manager within 45 minutes of your last check-out to say you are home. If you are stranded, stay somewhere safe and phone us; that time is paid.
Weather alerts reach you as a text asking you to phone in: phone as soon as you safely can, never while driving.
Acknowledge the hot weather briefing in CareFlow by 31 May, the cold weather briefing by 31 October, and this procedure within 14 days of each new major version.

blocks.p: Severe weather harms the people we support more than most: many are older, have long-term conditions or take medicines affecting how they cope with temperature, and cannot open a window or turn on the heating between visits. The same weather makes our care workers' journeys more dangerous.

{{organisation}} will check for alerts every day, know who is most at risk and what protects them, check temperatures and supplies in their homes, and keep essential care going without asking staff to make journeys they judge unsafe. When we cannot reach everyone, we protect those at greatest risk first and learn from every event.

This procedure applies the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) Adverse Weather and Health Plan and its social care guidance to home care. The law requires us to assess and reduce risks to people's safety, including medicines (Regulation 12), and to employees, identifying those especially at risk (Management of Health and Safety at Work Regulations 1999, regulation 3), and to notify CQC of events that threaten safe care (regulation 18(2)(g)). The temperatures, timescales and priorities here are our policy, based on UKHSA guidance.

This procedure applies to all staff, including bank and agency workers, and to every person we support. It covers heat, cold, snow and ice, flooding, storms and weather-related loss of power, heating or water, in people's homes and on the road.

Owned elsewhere: driving and winter vehicle kit (Driving at Work Policy); check-in monitoring (Lone Working and Staff Personal Safety Policy); late and missed visits and missed-visit risk levels (Missed, Late and Short Visits Procedure); disruption from any cause, including closure of a branch office (Business Continuity and Emergency Planning Policy); office temperatures (Health and Safety Policy); heaters and open fires (Fire Safety in People's Homes Policy); and dehydration (Nutrition and Hydration Policy).

rows: Weather-health alert

A UKHSA alert, issued with the Met Office: Heat-Health Alerts (core season 1 June to 30 September) and Cold-Health Alerts (core season 1 November to 31 March), with extraordinary alerts outside these seasons. Yellow: health risks mainly to vulnerable people. Amber: impacts likely across the health service, and the wider population may be at risk. Red: significant risk to life even for healthy people.
Weather warning
A yellow, amber or red Met Office warning for snow, ice, rain, wind, fog or extreme heat.
Flood warnings
Environment Agency flood alert (flooding is possible: prepare), flood warning (flooding is expected: act now) and severe flood warning (danger to life).
Higher weather risk
Our marker in My care at a glance for a person at greater risk from heat, cold or both: a medical alert titled Higher weather risk on their CareFlow record, which care workers see in the app.

blocks.p: The Directors fund the equipment, taxis, extra visits and staff pay this procedure sets out.

The Registered Manager is the severe weather lead, covered by the Deputy Manager. They keep alert registrations and seasonal readiness in place, lead each response and decide business continuity activation, extra visits and CQC notifications.

subsections.heading: Care Coordinators, Office staff and On-call Manager

blocks.p: Care Coordinators check and cascade alerts, keep the severe weather list, adjust rotas, arrange welfare calls and keep people, families and commissioners informed; Office staff make allocated welfare calls. Out of hours the On-call Manager does this and phones the escalation manager at once about any amber or red alert or warning, flood warning or visit at risk.

subsections.heading: Field Care Supervisors, assessors and HR Manager

blocks.p: Assessors set the higher weather risk marker. Field Care Supervisors give care when cover is needed. The HR Manager keeps staff contact details current.

subsections.heading: Senior Care Workers and Care Workers

blocks.p: Care workers make the visit checks, record them and phone the office when a threshold is reached. Phoning the office means speaking to a person at the branch office, or the On-call Manager out of hours; if nobody answers within 15 minutes, phone the Registered Manager or Deputy Manager directly.

The Registered Manager registers the branch office email account, and the Registered Manager's and Deputy Manager's work email, for UKHSA weather-health alerts for every region the branch serves and for Environment Agency flood warnings for the branch office and each flood warning area where we support people.

Each working day by 10am the Care Coordinator checks UKHSA weather-health alerts, Met Office warnings and flood warnings for every area the branch serves for the next 5 days, and records the result, including no alerts, on the daily office rota. The On-call Manager checks at the start of each on-call period and by 7am on weekend and bank holiday mornings. We act on the alert for the area where each person lives.

subsections.heading: Identifying people at higher weather risk

blocks.p: At assessment and every care plan review, the assessor completes the heating and temperature part of the home environment risk assessment under the Risk Assessment and Home Environment Risk Assessment Procedure. A person is at higher weather risk for heat, cold or both when any of these applies:

bullets: they are alone for long periods and cannot without help open windows, change the heating or clothing, or get a drink;
they cannot recognise or say they are too hot or cold, for example because of dementia;
they are 65 or over, or pregnant, and have a heart, breathing or kidney condition, diabetes or Parkinson's disease, or are mostly in bed;
their GP or pharmacist has told us a medicine they take increases their risk in heat or cold;
their home cannot be kept at a safe temperature or is in a flood risk area; or
they have a High missed-visit risk level and live alone.

blocks.p: The marker is shown in My care at a glance, with the person's controls in the visit plans. The Care Coordinator updates the severe weather list, held in the business continuity records for use if CareFlow is unavailable, the same working day a marker changes. Where a person uses powered medical equipment or is at higher weather risk, the assessor asks whether they are on their energy and water suppliers' Priority Services Registers and, with their agreement, the Care Coordinator helps them register within 10 working days.

sections.heading: Alert levels and how we respond

rows: Yellow Heat-Health or Cold-Health Alert; yellow Met Office warning for snow, ice, rain or wind; or flood alert for an area we serve
Weather watch

Within 2 hours of the alert reaching us and before the first affected visit, the Care Coordinator, or On-call Manager, texts every care worker rostered for the affected days asking them to phone in as soon as they safely can, never while driving (Mobile Phones and Social Media Policy), and tells each caller the alert, the checks to start and any rota change; anyone not heard from before their first affected visit is phoned. Travel time is increased on affected journeys.
Amber or red Heat-Health or Cold-Health Alert; amber or red Met Office warning; flood warning or severe flood warning for an area we serve; or reports that roads in our area are unsafe
Severe weather response
Weather watch actions plus the steps below, led by the Registered Manager.
Weather means that in the next 24 hours any visit is expected to be missed, shortened or moved outside its window, or 5 or more visits are expected to start more than 30 minutes late
Business continuity activation

The Registered Manager, or the On-call Manager through the escalation manager, activates the Business Continuity and Emergency Planning Policy, tells the Nominated Individual at once and protects visits in the order below.

blocks.p: Severe weather response steps:

steps: Within 2 hours in office hours, the Registered Manager holds a planning call with the Care Coordinators, a Field Care Supervisor and the HR Manager; out of hours, the On-call Manager and escalation manager agree the next 24 hours by phone. One incident log entry records every decision, the visits affected and who was told.

The Care Coordinator reviews the next 48 hours of the rota, and again each day by 2pm with the daily cover check: at least double the usual travel time on journeys affected by snow, ice or flooding, and local rounds so workers visit people near their homes.

The Care Coordinator confirms with the chosen contact of each person with a time-critical visit or a High missed-visit risk level, and each person at higher weather risk who lives alone, what help they could give if we are delayed.

For cold, snow, ice and flood triggers, by the end of the next working day the office confirms that each person in the affected area whose medicines we support has at least 7 days' supply and each person who relies on us for meals has at least 3 days' food and drink, arranging any shortfall the same working day.

Each person at higher weather risk who lives alone has contact every day of an amber or red heat or cold alert: their visit or an office welfare call, by 11am in cold weather and between 2pm and 5pm in hot weather. No answer follows the No Reply, No Access and Missing Person Procedure.

Where a person needs more care to stay safe, the Registered Manager or On-call Manager may add an extra welfare visit at once, agreed with the commissioner within 5 working days; a person paying for their own care is charged only with their agreement.

The Care Coordinator tells each affected commissioner the same working day. When alerts end and visits are back to normal, the Registered Manager stands the response down and tells staff and commissioners the same day.

sections.heading: Hot weather: what we do on visits

blocks.p: During a heat-health alert, at every visit:

bullets: For a person at higher weather risk, read the thermometer in the room they use most and record it in the daily visit notes.

With the person's agreement, close curtains on sunny windows, open windows only when it is cooler outside and the care plan says they can be left open safely, and secure any window the person cannot secure before you leave.
Use a fan only below 35°C, never aimed directly at the person's body.

Offer extra drinks and water-rich foods such as fruit, lollies and salads and, unless a health professional has restricted fluids, leave at least two full drinks within reach, one of them water. Phone the office before leaving about signs of dehydration, as the Nutrition and Hydration Policy sets out.
Help with light clothing and bedding and a cool wash, and keep the person out of the sun between 11am and 3pm.

Keep medicines below 25°C, out of the sun and off windowsills, and never in the fridge unless the label says so; if nowhere is cool enough, phone the office, which gets pharmacist advice the same day and updates the care plan.
Food left out for later is left no more than 2 hours on a very hot day, as the Food Hygiene Guideline sets out. Phone the office the same day if a person with a pain-relief patch feels very hot.

rows: Room above 26°C

Take the cooling actions and check again before leaving. If the person is at higher weather risk and it is still above 26°C, or you cannot keep them cool, phone the office before leaving; the Care Coordinator or On-call Manager decides the same day on a welfare call, extra visit, family help or GP advice.
Room 35°C or above

No fan. Phone the office before leaving for every person; the office makes contact again within 3 hours and the Registered Manager (On-call Manager out of hours) decides the same day on an extra visit.
Heat exhaustion: tiredness, dizziness, headache, nausea, heavy sweating with pale clammy skin, cramps, intense thirst

Move the person somewhere cooler, remove extra clothing, give water if they can swallow safely, and cool their skin with sprayed or sponged cool water and a wrapped cold pack under the armpits or on the neck. Stay, and phone the office, which gets NHS 111 advice if needed and covers your next visit.
Heatstroke: still unwell after 30 minutes of cooling, hot skin that is not sweating, fast breathing, confusion, a fit or loss of consciousness
Call 999, keep cooling them and follow the First Aid Procedure. Then phone the office.

blocks.p: Heat illness is entered in the incident log before the end of the shift and the Care Coordinator tells the GP the same day.

sections.heading: Cold weather, snow and ice: what we do on visits

blocks.p: In cold weather, at every visit:

bullets: During a cold-health alert, for a person at higher weather risk, read the living room thermometer and record it in the daily visit notes; UKHSA advises heating the rooms people use most to at least 18°C.

With the person's agreement, switch the heating on or up using only the controls the person normally uses, such as the switch, thermostat or timer. Never repair, reset or repressurise a boiler, light or refuel an open fire, stove, or gas or paraffin heater, or touch the fuse box.
If a prepayment meter has run out and the person cannot use it, you may switch on its emergency credit with their agreement, then phone the office before leaving.
Help with thin layers, blankets, a hot drink and, where we prepare meals, a hot meal each day if wanted. Use hot water bottles, heat packs and electric blankets only where the care plan allows.
Tell the office before leaving if food, drinks or medicines will run out before the next delivery.

On an icy path you may spread the person's own grit or salt with their agreement; otherwise tell the office, which asks the family or landlord to clear it. Free a frozen key safe only with de-icer, never hot water or force.

rows: Room below 18°C

Take the warming actions. Phone the office before leaving if the room is still below 18°C for a person at higher weather risk, or the person declines heating, it is not working or there is no credit or fuel. The Care Coordinator or On-call Manager contacts the family, landlord, supplier or local authority and agrees a safe way for the person to keep warm the same day. Possible self-neglect also goes to the safeguarding lead under the Self-Neglect and Hoarding Procedure.
Carbon monoxide alarm, or headache, dizziness, nausea or collapse in more than one person

Open doors and windows, help the person out if safe, call 999 if anyone is unwell and phone the office. Then follow the Fire Safety in People's Homes Policy, including the gas emergency call; nobody goes back in until the Registered Manager, Deputy Manager or On-call Manager says so.
Feels cold or is shivering, but is alert, talking normally and warming up

Warm the person gradually: warm room, blankets, dry clothing and a warm drink if they can swallow safely; no hot bath, hot water bottle, heat lamp, rubbing or alcohol. Phone the office before leaving.
Possible hypothermia: pale, cold, dry skin or blue or grey lips with slurred speech, slow breathing, unusual tiredness or confusion; unresponsive; or found cold on the floor

Call 999, cover them where they lie, warm them gradually as above and follow the First Aid Procedure and, for a person on the floor, the Falls Prevention and Response Procedure. Then phone the office.

blocks.p: Suspected hypothermia is entered in the incident log before the end of the shift and the Care Coordinator tells the GP the same day.

sections.heading: Flooding, storms and loss of power or water

rows: Flooding on your route
Never walk or drive through floodwater, however shallow. Turn back and phone the office.
Flood warning for a person's home

The Care Coordinator phones the person or chosen contact the same day to check where they would go, their medicines, equipment and a key holder. A person who could not leave unaided is reported to the local authority the same day, sharing only what is needed under the Confidentiality and Information Sharing Policy.
Severe flood warning or evacuation
Follow the emergency services. Help the person take their medicines, aids and the home copy of their care plan, and phone the office.
After flooding

Never switch on wet electrical items or gas appliances until an engineer has checked them. Wear gloves and an apron to handle anything floodwater touched, then wash your hands. Report damp, mould or distress to the office.
Amber or red wind warning

Park and walk away from trees and scaffolding, and keep clear of fallen power lines, reporting them on 105, or 999 if anyone is in danger. During any red warning, the Registered Manager or escalation manager agrees each journey before it is made.
Power cut during a visit

Check the person is safe and that their phone and pendant alarm work. Help with an oxygen back-up cylinder only as the care plan sets out and phone the supplier's emergency number. Never change the settings of an airflow mattress or other powered equipment; phone the office before leaving, and the office contacts the community nursing team or supplier the same day.
Power off at a person's home

The office reports it on 105, the national power cut number, and phones the person or contact at least every 4 hours until power returns; a person at higher weather risk who lives alone is visited within 4 hours. Where a fridge holding a medicine has lost power, the office gets pharmacist advice before the next dose, as the Ordering, Collecting, Storing and Disposing of Medicines Procedure sets out.
Water supply lost
The office makes sure the person has bottled drinking water the same day through family, the water supplier or our own purchase.

blocks.p: You decide whether a journey is safe for you. If you judge a route unsafe, do not travel: phone the office or On-call Manager as soon as you know which visits you cannot reach. Nobody may pressure or penalise you. A worker told not to travel, or who reports in good faith that a route is unsafe, is paid the planned visit and travel time unless given other work in the same time slot; contracted hours are always paid. The Care Coordinator offers other work where possible, such as visits nearer home or a taxi at our cost.

Free ice grips are available from the branch office from 1 November. During a severe weather response every care worker phones or texts the office or On-call Manager within 45 minutes of their last check-out, unless a longer journey time has been agreed, to say they are home, or the escalation in the Lone Working and Staff Personal Safety Policy starts. A stranded worker stays somewhere safe and warm, never runs a vehicle engine with the exhaust blocked by snow, and phones the office, which phones them at least hourly until they are home. Time stranded is paid.

Every care worker receives a free refillable water bottle at induction. In hot weather, drink between every visit and wear sunscreen and a hat when walking. During an amber or red heat-health alert, the Care Coordinator plans a break of at least 15 minutes somewhere cool at least every 3 hours of visits. Never go without the protective equipment the care plan or the Standard Infection Control Precautions Procedure requires, but change it when damp and carry spare stock. If you feel dizzy, confused or sick, stop, cool down and phone the office; do not drive, and we pay for a taxi.

Staff who are pregnant, have a heart, breathing or circulation condition or diabetes, or take a medicine affecting how they cope with heat or cold, are asked at each seasonal briefing to tell the HR Manager, who reviews their individual risk assessment with the Registered Manager within 5 working days; pregnancy follows the New and Expectant Mothers at Work Procedure. Adjustments, such as shorter runs or visits at cooler times, are recorded in the staff record, and Care Coordinators are told only the adjustment.

sections.heading: Protecting visits when not everyone can be reached

blocks.p: Once business continuity is activated, visits are protected in this order, using the severe weather list:

rows: Time-critical visits
Delivered within their window under the Time-Sensitive Medicines Protocol.
Other visits to people with a High missed-visit risk level
Delivered; the Registered Manager, Deputy Manager or On-call Manager goes if nobody else can safely reach the person.
Standard visits with essential tasks for people at higher weather risk
Delivered, late only with the person's agreement.
Other Standard visits with essential tasks
Moved only with the agreement of the person, or their chosen contact where they cannot decide.
Visits with no essential tasks, such as cleaning or shopping
Postponed first, with agreement, and rebooked within 7 days.

blocks.p: Only the Registered Manager, Deputy Manager or On-call Manager may agree that a visit is moved or shortened, always keeping every essential task. A visit we could not staff is never treated as a cancellation or charged, even with the person's agreement. A two-worker visit is never done by one worker. A family member gives named tasks only where they and the person agree, and a phone call never replaces a visit with essential tasks. If nobody can reach a person with a time-critical visit or High missed-visit risk level by any safe route, the manager asks their chosen contact to check on them, asks the local authority for a welfare check where no contact can, calls 999 where life may be at risk and keeps trying to get a worker there. Every attempt is recorded in the incident log entry for the event.

The office phones each person or chosen contact before a care worker will be more than 30 minutes late. While business continuity is active, the Care Coordinator sends each affected commissioner a written update by 12 noon daily, tells the GP or community nursing team the same day when a health task or time-critical medicine is affected, and co-ordinates with other agencies visiting the same person. The Registered Manager (Deputy Manager in their absence) notifies CQC as the Statutory Notifications to CQC Procedure requires.

Within 5 working days of stand-down, the Registered Manager reviews the event with the Care Coordinators and a Field Care Supervisor: alert timing, visits missed, late or moved, harm, illness, staff injuries and what worked. This is also the event-triggered risk review under the Risk Management Policy; actions go into the service improvement plan and the review to the next Health and Safety Meeting.
